title: Simulation studies for methodological research in psychology: A standardized template for planning, preregistration, and reporting.
abstract: Simulation studies are widely used for evaluating the performance of statistical methods in psychology. However, the quality of simulation studies can vary widely in terms of their design, execution, and reporting. In order to assess the quality of typical simulation studies in psychology, we reviewed 321 articles published in Psychological Methods, Behavior Research Methods, and Multivariate Behavioral Research in 2021 and 2022, among which 100/321 = 31.2% report a simulation study. We find that many articles do not provide complete and transparent information about key aspects of the study, such as justifications for the number of simulation repetitions, Monte Carlo uncertainty estimates, or code and data to reproduce the simulation studies. To address this problem, we provide a summary of the ADEMP (aims, data-generating mechanism, estimands and other targets, methods, performance measures) design and reporting framework from Morris et al. (2019) adapted to simulation studies in psychology. Based on this framework, we provide ADEMP-PreReg, a step-by-step template for researchers to use when designing, potentially preregistering, and reporting their simulation studies. We give formulae for estimating common performance measures, their Monte Carlo standard errors, and for calculating the number of simulation repetitions to achieve a desired Monte Carlo standard error. Finally, we give a detailed tutorial on how to apply the ADEMP framework in practice using an example simulation study on the evaluation of methods for the analysis of pre-post measurement experiments. title: Reporting Practices, Open Science Practices, and Trustworthiness of Simulation Studies in Psychology: A Questionnaire Study
abstract: Simulation studies have received little attention in the replication crisis. This exploratory study investigated reporting practices, open science practices, and trustworthiness of simulation studies in psychology. 221 researchers (response rate=35.1%) completed a questionnaire about one simulation-based article they authored in 2023-2024. Authors reported at least some selective or fragmented reporting of conditions, methods, and performance measures in 50.2% of the articles (i.e., omitting results completely or split between the main text and supplements). Reporting nonconvergence and Monte Carlo Standard Errors was uncommon, likely due to limited awareness and weakly established norms. 19% of articles were neutral (i.e., authors did not develop the evaluated methods), but selective and fragmented reporting was not lower in these studies. Over 75% of authors reported sharing their complete code, but measures for reproducibility like providing instructions (39.6%) and independent code checking (20.3%) were uncommon. Guidelines were not used because researchers were unaware of them, perceived them as unnecessary, or considered them uncommon. These prevalence estimates should, however, be interpreted with caution, as self-report and self-selection bias may have led to overly optimistic estimates. Respondents estimated the probability that conclusions of a typical simulation study are trustworthy to be .74, exceeding estimates for computational reproducibility (.64) and complete reporting (.55). As responsible reporting standards and code-sharing were not standard, we recommend journals to endorse reporting standards such as ADEMP (Morris et al., 2019), use standardized repositories and workflows for sharing materials, and check code availability. Keywords: simulation studies, reproducibility, replicability, open science, QRPs, selective reporting, trustworthiness

title: Transparent reporting items for simulation studies evaluating statistical methods: Foundations for reproducibility and reliability
abstract: Abstract Simulation studies are essential tools to assess statistical methods. Functioning as controlled experiments, simulations generate data from known underlying processes. However, unclear or incomplete reporting of simulation studies can impact their interpretability and reproducibility, potentially leading to the misuse of statistical methods. While Morris et al. (2019, Stat Med, 38, p. 2074) recently provided guidance on the planning and conduct of simulation studies for statistical method evaluation, there is currently no comprehensive set of reporting guidelines in ecology and evolutionary biology. Here, we propose 11 reporting items for statistical simulation studies extending on Morris and colleagues' guidance. These items span across three stages: planning, coding and analysis. We also clarify the terminology related to statistical components and the broad purposes of statistical simulation studies. To highlight our proposed reporting items with current practices, we surveyed 100 articles in ecology and evolution journals that included a simulation study evaluating a statistical method. Our survey found room for improvement in more transparent reporting to ensure clear evaluation of statistical methods. Most notably, only a small proportion of articles reported a Monte Carlo uncertainty (17%; 17 out of 98), and 32% (32 out of 100) articles did not provide code. Beyond the proposed reporting items, we discuss the benefits of open science tools to enhance the reproducibility of simulation studies. Specifically, we propose the registration of statistical simulation studies to enhance planning, reporting and collaboration. We aim to instigate discussions to improve the reporting of simulation studies for statistical method research. The reporting items we propose, along with open science tools, serve as a template for developing standards and guidelines for simulation studies evaluating statistical methods. These reporting guidelines will help enhance reproducibility and indirectly encourage more consideration in the design and conduct of these simulation studies.

title: An Extended Nonvisual Approach for the Screening for Nonstationarity in Multivariate Time Series Data
abstract: Zitzmann et al. (2025) introduced a nonvisual screening procedure for nonstationarity in univariate time series. The present project builds on that work by extending the procedure to the application to multivariate time series data. The procedure is thus intended as a tool for assessing multivariate (rather than solely univariate) nonstationarity. In general, weak (or second-order) univariate stationarity, which is most commonly studied in time series analysis, refers to time-invariance of the mean, variance, and innovation autocovariance. In other words, the expected level of the variable as well as its variance and innovation autocovariance should not increase or decrease over time. The same holds for multivariate stationarity, but it extends this concept to between-series properties as well, namely the contemporaneous covariance between innovations and the lagged covariance between innovations from different variables. Therefore, multivariate stationarity is generally defined by two conditions: 1) the mean vector is independent of time t, and 2) the covariance matrix is independent of time t for every lag h. Consequently, multivariate nonstationarity is given if at least one of these conditions is violated. Notably, multivariate nonstationarity can even occur if all properties of individual time series (means, variances, and autocovariances) are stationary, since covariances between the series have to be considered too. This is why nonstationarity screening of each series separately is generally insufficient for detecting multivariate nonstationarity. To assess these aspects practically, five indicators were created, each reflecting one aspect of multivariate nonstationarity: a) trends (changes in means over time), b) changes in variances over time (lag h = 0), c) changes in autocorrelations (AR) over time (lag h ≠0), d) changes in contemporaneous correlations over time (lag h = 0), and e) changes in lagged correlations over time (lag h ≠ 0). We will conduct a simulation study in which both the properties of the individual time series (trend, change in variance, and change in AR) as well as the between-series properties of the time series (changes in the correlations and lagged correlations between time series) will be varied. We will then evaluate the performance of the indicators in detecting these aspects of multivariate nonstationarity. This preregistration loosely follows the ADEMP (Aims, Data-generating mechanism, Estimands and other targets, Methods, Performance measures) design and reporting framework by Morris et al. (2019) and the adaptation to simulation studies in psychology by Siepe et al. (2024).

title: Preregistration - "Reporting Practices, Open Science Practices, and Trustworthiness of Simulation Studies in Psychology: A Questionnaire Study"
abstract: Monte Carlo simulation studies in which statistical methods are evaluated, are widespread in scientific literature. Surprisingly, they have received remarkably little attention from a meta-research perspective. Those studies that did investigate the current state of replicability, reproducibility, and reporting standards in simulation studies often argue for reform of standard practices to improve their quality (e.g., Luijken et al., 2024; Morris et al., 2019; Pawel et al., 2024). To date, however, no study has examined the prevalence and motivations for selective reporting and uptake of open science practices in simulation studies, specifically among researchers who have themselves conducted simulation studies. Moreover, no previous literature has investigated the trust researchers have in simulation studies conducted by others in their field. This study sets out to increase our understanding in these areas. This exploratory study investigates the prevalence and motivations for selective reporting, adherence to open science practices, and reasons for non-adherence in simulation studies in psychology that evaluate statistical methods. We also examine the level of trust in simulation studies conducted by others in the field, among researchers who have themselves conducted at least one such study. This preregistration serves as a guide for both the authors and readers in conducting and evaluating the analyses. While we aim to be as transparent as possible in outlining our analysis decisions and protocols prior to data collection, the exploratory nature of this study implies that additional analyses will be conducted next to the preregistered analyses. Any additions to the preregistered analyses will be documented in the final publication.
authors: Marcel A. L. M. van Assen

title: Simulation Studies for Methodological Research in Psychology
abstract: Our overall goal is to assess the design and reporting standards of simulation studies in methodological psychology journals. Following a previous study by Morris et al. (2019), we will review aims, data-generating processes, estimands, methods, and performance measures (“ADEMP”) as well as the reporting of results. Building on the literature review, we will design a pre registration template for simulation studies. We will then showcase this template in a small simulation study of our own.
